title: Area III review: Airspace and VFR Rules
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area III: airspace classes and equipment, VFR weather minimums and special VFR, special use airspace and TFRs, and minimum safe altitudes and speed limits. Many join two of them in one real flight, the way a reviewing instructor would ask.

questions.q: You fly a fast single-engine turboprop toward a Class C primary airport (elevation 500 ft). You are 7 NM out, inside the shelf, level at 3,000 ft MSL at 230 KIAS. You call approach and hear "N45TP, standby." What is true?
options: You may continue in, at up to 250 KIAS for now; once within 4 NM of the airport and at or below 2,500 ft above the surface, slow to 200 KIAS or less
You must stay outside: "standby" means ATC has not yet accepted you
You may continue in, but 200 KIAS is the limit anywhere inside Class C
You must hold outside until ATC says "cleared into the Class C"
questions.why: A reply that uses your call sign, even "standby," establishes two-way radio communication, so you may enter [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]] [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]]. Class C needs no clearance. The 200-knot limit covers only the airspace at or below 2,500 ft above the surface within 4 NM of the primary airport [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]. At 7 NM you are outside that box, so the general limit is 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft MSL [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]. Thinking 200 knots covers the whole Class C is the tempting mistake.

questions.q: A part-time Class D tower is closed for the night, and the Chart Supplement says "other times CLASS G." The chart shows the Class E above beginning at 1,200 ft AGL. The weather is broken clouds at 1,300 ft AGL with 4 SM visibility. You want to fly night landings in a 1,000 ft AGL pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway. Is it legal?
options: Yes: in a Class G traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway you only need to stay clear of clouds
No: at night in Class G with 3 SM or more you need 500 ft below the clouds, and a 1,000 ft pattern is only 300 ft below them
No: the 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM rules of the surface area still apply when the tower closes
Yes: the ceiling is above 1,000 ft and the visibility is at least 3 SM
questions.why: With the tower closed the surface area is Class G up to the overlying Class E [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5a2]], so the pattern at 1,000 ft AGL is in Class G. At night there, below 1,200 ft AGL, you need 3 SM and 500 ft below clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. 1,300 minus 1,000 leaves only 300 ft. The clear-of-clouds pattern rule applies only when the visibility is less than 3 SM but at least 1 SM [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)]], so it does not help at 4 SM. The 1,000-and-3 rules apply only in controlled airspace designated to the surface [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)-(d)]], and meeting them would not fix the cloud clearance anyway.

questions.q: In a fast turboprop single you depart a Class B primary airport with a clearance. Which speed plan fits 91.117?
options: 200 KIAS until you are more than 4 NM from the airport, then 250 KIAS
250 KIAS everywhere below 10,000 ft MSL, inside or under the Class B
Up to 250 KIAS while inside the Class B; 200 KIAS if you go below a shelf floor or into a VFR corridor; no 91.117 limit at or above 10,000 ft MSL
200 KIAS anywhere inside the Class B lateral limits, at any altitude
questions.why: The 200-knot rule near Class C and D airports does not apply inside Class B. There, the 250-knot limit below 10,000 ft MSL applies [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)-(b)]]. Underneath a Class B, or in a VFR corridor through it, the limit is 200 KIAS [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]]. 91.117(a) sets no limit at or above 10,000 ft MSL. Using 200 knots out to 4 NM is the tempting error. It borrows the Class C and D rule, which the regulation says does not apply in Class B.

questions.q: Cleared into Class B, you cruise at 4,500 ft MSL with 4 SM visibility. A cloud base sits at 4,800 ft MSL. Your route will soon leave the Class B sideways into Class E at the same altitude. What is true?
options: You are legal now, but in Class E you need 500 ft below the clouds. Before you leave the Class B, tell ATC and be at 4,300 ft MSL or lower
You are not legal now: Class B also needs 500 ft below clouds
You are legal now and after you leave, because ATC assigned the altitude
You are legal now; in Class E you need 1,000 ft below clouds, so be at 3,800 ft MSL
questions.why: In Class B the VFR rule is 3 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]], so 300 ft below the base is legal there. Class E below 10,000 ft MSL needs 500 ft below clouds: 4,800 minus 500 is 4,300 ft MSL. When an assigned altitude would break weather minimums, tell approach and get a revised clearance [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3e]]. ATC's altitude assignment does not lift 91.155. The 1,000 ft below figure is for Class E at or above 10,000 ft MSL.

questions.q: Your VFR route crosses IR1206 at 1,200 ft AGL on a clear day. What should you expect?
options: No military traffic: IR routes are flown only when the weather is IFR
Traffic only above 1,500 ft AGL, since a four-digit route has at least one high segment
Fast military traffic may be at your altitude: no segment of a four-digit route is above 1,500 ft AGL, and IR routes are flown under IFR whatever the weather. Ask an FSS within 100 NM about activity
You need a clearance from the route's scheduling unit before you cross an active IR route
questions.why: Four digits mean no segment above 1,500 ft AGL [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2d]]. IR routes are flown under IFR regardless of weather, so a clear day does not mean the route is quiet [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2c]]. MTRs are generally for speeds above 250 knots [[33:193|AIM 3-5-2c]]. You may fly through an MTR with extreme vigilance, and an FSS within 100 NM can give you current use and route width [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2g]]. No clearance is needed to cross one.

questions.q: On special VFR you depart a Class D airport (elevation 600 ft). It reports overcast at 900 ft and 2 SM. A town lies straight ahead off the runway, and its highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is 200 ft AGL. Open farmland lies to either side. What is your plan?
options: Cross the town at 1,500 ft MSL, because the takeoff exception in 91.119 covers your climbout
Turn over the farmland and stay between 1,100 ft MSL and the cloud base. Over the town you would need 1,800 ft MSL, which is in the clouds
Climb to 1,800 ft MSL over the town; special VFR allows brief cloud contact
Cross the town at any altitude below the clouds; on SVFR, ATC is responsible for obstacle clearance
questions.why: Special VFR requires clear of clouds and 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]]. The cloud base is 600 + 900 = 1,500 ft MSL. Over the town, 91.119(b) needs 600 + 200 + 1,000 = 1,800 ft MSL. Over farmland, 91.119(c) needs 600 + 500 = 1,100 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)-(c)]]. On SVFR the pilot is responsible for obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. The "except when necessary for takeoff or landing" phrase covers only the low flight you need to take off or land [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. A town you can turn away from is not necessary.

questions.q: Your route: depart a nontowered Class G field, pass through a Class D surface area, fly under a Class B shelf about 20 NM from its Appendix D, section 1 airport, then land at a nontowered satellite airport inside a Class C. Which list is right?
options: Class D: an ATC clearance. Under the shelf: a Class B clearance. Class C: two-way radio with the tower at the satellite
Class D: two-way radio contact before entry. Under the shelf: nothing, because the veil rules apply only inside Class B. Class C: ADS-B Out only

Class D: two-way radio contact before entry. Under the shelf: Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out, no clearance. Class C: two-way radio contact with the Class C facility before entry, and the FAA arrival pattern at the satellite
Class D: nothing for VFR. Under the shelf: Mode C transponder only. Class C: a clearance from approach
questions.why: Class D needs two-way radio communication established before entry [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(1)]]. Under the shelf you are outside the Class B, so no clearance is needed [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]], but you are inside the 30 NM veil, where a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required from the surface to 10,000 ft MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]]. Class C needs two-way radio communication before entry and its transponder and ADS-B equipment, and landing at a satellite follows the FAA arrival and departure patterns [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(b)-(c)]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.130(d)]]. The veil is the item most often missed.

questions.q: A wildfire TFR under 91.137(a)(2) runs from the surface to 3,500 ft MSL on your course line. Terrain is 1,000 ft MSL and your magnetic course is 200°. You plan to stay VFR and cross over the top. Which statement is true?
options: 91.159 applies to all VFR cruise, so you must cruise at 4,500 or 6,500 ft MSL
From just above 3,500 up to 4,000 ft MSL you are not more than 3,000 ft above the surface, so 91.159 does not apply; above that, the first fitting altitude is 4,500 ft MSL
On a 200° course the correct altitude is 5,500 ft MSL
You may not cross over a disaster relief TFR at any altitude
questions.why: 91.159 applies only in level cruise more than 3,000 ft above the surface [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]]. 1,000 + 3,000 = 4,000 ft MSL, so below that you may cruise at any altitude. Above it, a magnetic course of 180° to 359° takes even thousands plus 500, so 4,500 ft MSL [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. 5,500 is the odd-plus-500 rule for 0° to 179°. The TFR covers only the area and altitudes its NOTAM gives [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]], so flying above its top is not flying in it [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)]]. The sources give no buffer distance, so leave a sensible margin.

questions.q: A NOTAM sets a 91.137(a)(1) TFR around a chemical spill: 5 NM radius, surface to 3,000 ft AGL. Your course crosses it at 2,500 ft AGL. A friend says TFRs are "2,000 ft and 3 NM," and that ATC can clear you through anyway. What is true?
options: You are above the normal 2,000 ft top, so you are clear
You may enter if approach control authorizes it
You may enter if you notify the FSS named in the NOTAM and are not there to observe
You may not enter: the NOTAM's numbers apply, only relief aircraft under the on-scene official may fly in an (a)(1) area, and ATC may authorize entry on its own only for (a)(2) and (a)(3) TFRs
questions.why: An (a)(1) TFR allows only aircraft taking part in the relief work under the direction of the official in charge on scene [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]]. ATC may authorize flight in a TFR on its own authority only for (a)(2) and (a)(3) TFRs [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3h]]. 2,000 ft and 3 NM is only the normal size [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3f]]. The NOTAM sets the real limits [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3i]], and here 2,500 ft AGL is inside them. The notify-the-FSS option is one of the (a)(2) conditions [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)]], not an (a)(1) one.

questions.q: You are 9 NM from a Class C primary airport, under its shelf, at 1,000 ft AGL in Class G, by day. Visibility is 2 SM and you are clear of clouds. Approach answers your call with your call sign. May you climb up into the shelf on your way in?
options: Yes: communication is established, and that is all Class C requires
No: communication is established, but Class C needs 3 SM and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft beside clouds. Stay in the Class G below
Yes, if you also stay clear of clouds
No: you need a clearance into Class C first
questions.why: A reply with your call sign establishes communication [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4c3]], so the radio rule is met. But the VFR weather minimums still apply: Class C needs 3 SM and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. In Class G by day at or below 1,200 ft AGL, 1 SM and clear of clouds is enough, which is why you are legal now. Class C never requires a clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]].

questions.q: Day, Class G, over farmland at 600 ft AGL. Visibility is 1.5 SM and an overcast sits at 900 ft AGL, getting lower. A town lies ahead, and its highest obstacle within 2,000 ft of your path is 150 ft AGL. What should you do?
options: Turn back or divert now. You are legal here, but over the town you would need 1,150 ft AGL, which is in the clouds
Continue over the town at 800 ft AGL; Class G only needs 1 SM and clear of clouds
Descend to 400 ft AGL to see better and continue
Continue; if you go into the cloud for a moment, climb and call ATC for a clearance on top
questions.why: Day Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL needs 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]], and 600 ft AGL over farmland meets the 500 ft rule [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(c)]]. Over the town you need 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft: 150 + 1,000 = 1,150 ft AGL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]], higher than the 900 ft base. Meeting the weather rule does not cancel 91.119. AC 91-92 says do not continue VFR into IMC; wait it out or turn around when weather drops below your limits, and do not go on top hoping for a hole [[37:15|AC 91-92 8.2]].

questions.q: Over a city, the ground is 500 ft MSL and the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft is 400 ft AGL. The only open field is 16,000 ft ahead. Your POH glide ratio is 10 to 1. You plan 1,900 ft MSL. What is true, in still air?
options: Both 91.119(a) and (b) are met at 1,900 ft MSL
(b) is met, but (a) is not: from 1,400 ft AGL you glide about 14,000 ft, short of the field. You need at least 1,600 ft AGL (2,100 ft MSL) before any margin
(a) applies only over open country, so (b) is all that matters over a city
Neither is met: (b) requires 2,400 ft MSL here
questions.why: 91.119(b): 500 + 400 + 1,000 = 1,900 ft MSL [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(b)]]. 91.119(a) applies everywhere and asks whether an engine failure leaves an emergency landing without undue hazard [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]]. A 10 to 1 glide ratio means 10 ft forward for each foot lost [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. 1,400 ft AGL x 10 = 14,000 ft, short of 16,000 ft. 16,000 / 10 = 1,600 ft AGL, which is 2,100 ft MSL, and wind and turns would need more. 2,400 ft MSL comes from wrongly adding the ground elevation twice.

questions.q: You want touch-and-go landings at a towered airport inside the DC SFRA, not in the FRZ. Which is correct?
options: Squawk 1200 while you stay in the pattern, since you never leave the airport area
Report your position on CTAF and squawk the discrete code from your SFRA flight plan
Squawk 1205 and monitor 121.5; no ATC contact is needed
Before departure, ask to remain in the pattern, stay in two-way contact with the tower, monitor 121.5 if equipped, and squawk 1234 unless ATC assigns another code
questions.why: At a towered SFRA airport, 93.339(d) requires a request to remain in the pattern, two-way contact with the tower, a 121.5 watch if equipped, and code 1234 unless ATC assigns another [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(d)]]. No one may squawk 1200 in the SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]]. CTAF reports and a pattern flight plan are the nontowered procedure [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(c)]]. 1205 is for departures from the fringe airports. Flying VFR within 60 NM of DCA also requires the Special Awareness Training [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].

questions.q: Your VFR route crosses an active MOA at 7,500 ft MSL. What is true?
options: No clearance is needed, but military jets there may fly faster than 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft. Check status with an FSS within 100 miles and call the controlling agency for traffic advisories before you enter
You need the controlling agency's permission, the same as for a restricted area
Military aircraft must also stay at or below 250 KIAS below 10,000 ft, so normal scanning is enough
Active MOAs are closed to VFR traffic
questions.why: MOAs are nonregulatory special use airspace [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1c]], so VFR pilots may enter, with extreme caution [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]]. The Department of Defense is authorized above 250 knots below 10,000 ft MSL in active MOAs [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5b]], even though 91.117(a) holds everyone else to 250 [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]. The AIM asks you to call an FSS within 100 miles for real-time status and the controlling agency for traffic advisories [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]]. Permission is needed for a restricted area [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]], not a MOA.

questions.q: On a magnetic course of 095° you want to cruise VFR at least 3,000 ft above a ridge at 7,800 ft MSL, in Class E. What is the lowest altitude that fits, and what does it need?
options: 10,500 ft MSL; 3 SM and 500 ft below clouds; no extra equipment
11,500 ft MSL; 5 SM, 1,000 ft below and above clouds and 1 SM beside them; a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out
11,500 ft MSL; 3 SM and 500 ft below clouds; a transponder only
12,500 ft MSL; 5 SM and 1,000 ft below clouds; no extra equipment, because you are over high terrain
questions.why: 7,800 + 3,000 = 10,800 ft MSL. A course of 0° to 179° takes odd thousands plus 500 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]], and 9,500 is too low, so 11,500 ft MSL. At or above 10,000 ft MSL, Class E needs 5 SM, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. You are 3,700 ft above the ridge, more than 2,500 ft above the surface, so the 10,000 ft MSL transponder and ADS-B Out rules apply [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]. 10,500 is an even altitude, which is for westbound courses.

questions.q: Your airplane's ADS-B Out failed this morning; the Mode C transponder works. The direct route home crosses over a Class C (ceiling 4,800 ft MSL) at 6,500 ft MSL, within its lateral limits, far from any Class B. You won't talk to approach. What is true?
options: Nothing is required: above the ceiling you are outside the Class C
Only a transponder is needed above a Class C; ADS-B Out matters only inside it

ADS-B Out is required there up to 10,000 ft MSL. Ask the ATC facility with jurisdiction for a deviation, which for an inoperative unit going to your destination or a repair place may be asked at any time, or route around
You must ask for the deviation at least 1 hour before the flight
questions.why: Above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of a Class C, up to 10,000 ft MSL, both a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out are required [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]]. No radio contact is needed there. For an inoperative ADS-B Out going to the destination or a place for repairs, the request may be made at any time. The 1-hour rule is for an aircraft not equipped with ADS-B Out [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]].

questions.q: Northbound in the Hudson River Exclusion, your fast single cruises at 165 KIAS. Which set of rules applies?
options: 200 KIAS or less, because you are under the Class B
140 KIAS or less, anticollision and position lights on if equipped, a current New York TAC aboard, and self-announce type, position, direction and altitude at the mandatory reporting points
140 KIAS or less, and a Class B clearance from New York approach before entering
250 KIAS or less, and landing lights on
questions.why: The exclusion's rules are 140 KIAS or less, anticollision and position lights on if equipped, self-announcing on the charted frequency and a current New York TAC [[60:709|14 CFR 93.351(a)-(d)]], plus reports at the mandatory reporting points [[60:709|14 CFR 93.352(a)]]. 91.117(c) does set 200 knots under a Class B [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]], but the 140-knot rule is lower, so it governs. You fly below the Class B floor [[60:709|14 CFR 93.352(c)]], so no Class B clearance is involved. Landing lights are only recommended.

questions.q: Sunset is 1830 and evening civil twilight ends at 1858. At 1840 you reach a Class D airport reporting overcast 700 ft and 2 SM. You hold a private certificate with no instrument rating. What can you do?
options: Ask for special VFR; for fixed-wing SVFR, day lasts until civil twilight ends at 1858
Land VFR; the 1,000 ft ceiling rule applies only at night
Divert: basic VFR is out (ceiling under 1,000 ft, visibility under 3 SM), and fixed-wing SVFR ended at sunset for a pilot who is not instrument qualified
Ask for special VFR; ATC may grant it any time traffic permits
questions.why: In the surface area you may not fly VFR beneath a ceiling under 1,000 ft, or land with less than 3 SM [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)-(d)]], day or night. Fixed-wing special VFR is allowed only between sunrise and sunset unless the pilot meets the part 61 instrument requirements and the airplane is equipped under 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. The civil twilight line is the 14 CFR 1.1 definition of night [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1 Night]] and is used for the 91.155 table, not for SVFR.

questions.q: On an IFR flight plan, your route crosses a joint-use restricted area. What will ATC do?
options: If the area is active and not released to the FAA, ATC will clear you around it; if it is inactive and released, ATC lets you through without a specific clearance for it
An IFR clearance always lets you fly through restricted areas
ATC never routes you around it; you must call the using agency yourself
Restricted areas are closed to IFR traffic at all times
questions.why: For joint-use restricted airspace, an area that is not active and has been released to the FAA can be flown without a specific clearance for it. An active area that has not been released gets a clearance that avoids it [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3b]]. An IFR clearance is not permission into an active area. That permission comes only from the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]]. Flying VFR, you get it from that agency yourself.

questions.q: A 91.137(a)(3) TFR surrounds a crash site 10 NM from your home field. Your passenger wants a look, and you think, "These TFR rules are silly. One quick pass won't hurt anybody." What is true?
options: That is macho; its antidote is "Taking chances is foolish." The pass is legal if you stay 1,000 ft above the obstacles
That is anti-authority; its antidote is "Follow the rules. They are usually right." The TFR bars flights made to observe the incident
That is impulsivity; its antidote is "Not so fast. Think first." The pass is legal if you tell Flight Service
That is resignation; its antidote is "I'm not helpless." Only ATC can decide whether you may enter
questions.why: Treating rules as silly or unnecessary is the anti-authority attitude, and its antidote is "Follow the rules. They are usually right" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. In an (a)(3) TFR, even the allowed flights to or from an airport inside may not be made to observe the incident [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)]]. TFR incursions have led to security investigations and certificate suspensions [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]]. Macho is about proving yourself to others, which is not the thought here.

questions.q: A towered airport sits in Class G airspace, with no Class D. The Class E above begins at 1,200 ft AGL. By day, visibility is 2 SM and you are clear of clouds. You plan to land there. What is true?
options: You may not land VFR: an airport with a tower always needs 3 SM
You may land; two-way radio contact with the tower must be established before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL, and Class G by day below 1,200 ft AGL needs 1 SM and clear of clouds
You may land without calling, because Class G has no radio rules
You need special VFR, because the visibility is under 3 SM
questions.why: Some towered airports are in Class G, so check the Chart Supplement [[1:386|PHAK 15-11]]. At any airport with an operating tower, 91.126(d) requires two-way radio contact, established before 4 NM, up to and including 2,500 ft AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]]. The 3 SM rule of 91.155(d) is for surface areas of Class B, C, D or E [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]], and special VFR exists only there [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]]. Class G by day at or below 1,200 ft AGL needs 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

questions.q: Your route crosses a MOA and a VR route, and you call 1-800-WX-BRIEF for a standard briefing. What should you do about their NOTAMs?
options: Nothing: a standard briefing includes every special use airspace NOTAM
Ask for them: MOA and MTR NOTAMs are upon-request items. Restricted area NOTAMs, P-40, P-49, P-56 and the DC SFRA are in the standard briefing
Nothing: MOA and MTR status is never available from Flight Service
Ask ATC once airborne; Flight Service gives MTR information only to military pilots
questions.why: A standard briefing gives NOTAM (D) items, including restricted area SUA NOTAMs, plus P-40, P-49, P-56 and the DC SFRA. MOA, MTR and warning area NOTAMs are upon-request items [[34:67|AIM 7-1-5]]. MTR information is available to pilots through Flight Service [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2f]], and an FSS within 100 miles can give MOA status [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5c]]. Expecting the briefer to cover everything is the trap.
